questions.q: Numbers are to be formed between $1000$ and $3000$, which are divisible by $4$, using the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$~and $6$& without repetition of digits. Then the total number of such numbers is _______.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
To find total numbers between $1000$ and $3000$ divisible by $4$ using the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$,

We will solve~in two cases.

Case I : When first digit is $1$.

Then last two digits can be $24, 32, 36, 52, 56$~or~$64$

So, total ways of choosing last two digit is~$6$~and second digit will be~chosen in~$3$~ways

So, number of such numbers $= 6 \times 3 = 18$

Case II: When first digit is $2$

Then last two digits can be $16, 36, 56$~or $64$

So, total ways of choosing last two digit is~$4$~and~second digit will be chosen in~$3$~

So, number of such numbers $= 4 \times 3 = 12$

Total numbers of numbers $= 18 + 12 = 30$

questions.q: The number of& $5$-digit natural numbers, such that the product of their digits is~$36$, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let the five digit number be $abcde$

$∵ 36 = {2}^{2} \times {3}^{2}$

Case I: When exactly one digit is $1$

So, number of~permutations of \left(2, 2, 3, 3, 1\right)$~will be

~$= \dfrac{5 !}{2 ! 2 !} = 30$

Case II: When exactly two digits are $1$

So, number of~permutations of \left(4, 3, 3, 1, 1\right), \left(6, 2, 3, 1, 1\right)$~or~ \left(9, 2, 2, 1, 1\right)$~will be

$= $\dfrac{5 !}{2 ! 2 !} + \dfrac{5 !}{2 !} + \dfrac{5 !}{2 ! 2 !} =$120$

Case III: When exactly three digits are $1$

So, number of~permutations of \left(4, 9, 1, 1, 1\right)$ or \left($6, 6, 1, 1, 1\right)$~will be

$= \dfrac{5 !}{3 !} + \dfrac{5 !}{3 ! 2 !} =30$

Hence, the required numbers$= 30 + 120 + 30 = 180

$

questions.q: The number of $4$-digit numbers which are neither multiple of $7$ nor multiple of $3$ is& <u>& & & & & & </u> .
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The total possible& $4$~digit numbers are~$9 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 9000$

Let, $X$ is the~$4$~digit number divisible by~$3$

$1002, 1005, \ldots \ldots \ldots , 9999$

$a = 1002, d = 3 \text{ and } {a}_{n} = 9999$

$9999 = 1002 + \left({n}_{3} - 1\right)3$

${n}_{3} = 3000$

Let, $Y$ is the~$4$~digit numbers divisible by $7$

$1001, 1008, \ldots \ldots \ldots , 9996$

$a = 1001, d = 7 \text{ and } {a}_{n} = 9996$

$9996 = 1001 + \left({n}_{7} - 1\right)7$

${n}_{7} = 1286$

Now,~$4$~digit~numbers divisible by both $3$ and $7$

$1008, 1029, . . . . . . . . . . . 9996$

$a = 1008, d = 21, {a}_{n} = 9996$

Now,~$9996 = 1008 + \left(n - 1\right)21$

$n = 429$

Hence, $4$~digit numbers neither divisible by $7$ nor $3$

$= 9000 - 1286 - 3000 + 429$

$= 5143$

Now,

$54 = 2 \times {3}^{3}$

So, for getting gcd with~$2$, we must have numbers multiple of~$2$~but not of~$3$.

Multiple of~$2$~are~\left\{1000, 1002, . . . . . , 9998\right\}$

Let total numbers be~$m$, then

$9998 = 1000 + \left(m - 1\right)2$

$⇒ m = 4500$

Total numbers are~$4500$.

Multiple of~$6$~are~\left\{1002, 1008 . . . . , 9996\right\}$

Let total numbers be~$n$, then

$9996 = 1002 + \left(n - 1\right)6$

$⇒ n = 1500$

So, required number is~$= 4500 - 1500 = 3000$

$

questions.q: The total number of $4$-digit numbers whose greatest common divisor with $18$ is $3$& is _____.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $N$ be the four digit number $gcd\left(N, 18\right) = 3$

Hence $N$ is an odd integer which is divisible by $3$ but not by $9$.

$4$ digit odd multiples of $3$

$1005, 1011, \ldots , 9999 \to 1500$

digit odd multiples of $9$

$1017, 1035, \ldots , 9999 \to 500$

Hence number of such $N = 1500 - 500 = 1000$
